statement: In Swedish men who had never smoked, snus use compared with using no tobacco is associated with a higher rate of death from any cause in the largest pooled cohort analysis read here (eight cohorts, 169,103 men, 10,928 deaths, about 17 years of follow-up on average, editors' calculation): adjusted for age and body mass index only, the hazard ratio for men who used snus and no other tobacco was 1.28 (95% CI 1.20–1.35), for cardiovascular deaths 1.27 (1.15–1.41), for cancer deaths 1.12 (1.00–1.26) and for deaths from other causes 1.37 (1.24–1.52) (Byhamre et al., 2021; funded by a university department, Swedish regional authorities and a medical society; no conflicts declared). The paper prints deaths by group but no rates per person-year, and the groups differed (men who used snus were younger, mean age 29 against 38, and more often in the highest alcohol tertile, 37.9% against 20.2%), so the ratios cannot be turned into a number out of 100. The ratio rose with years of use (1.08 under 5 years, 1.29 at 15 years or more) but not clearly with weekly amount; it was 1.42 (1.21–1.66) without the construction-worker cohort, which supplied 87% of the deaths in the snus group (editors' arithmetic); and the cardiovascular ratio was 1.13 (0.93–1.38) with follow-up capped at 10 years, which the authors say calls for caution. For cancers, an independent systematic review of 15 studies that left out work linked to the tobacco industry (Valen et al., 2023; no funding statement on the page; no conflicts declared) gave, in its summary table and per 100,000 men (the snus figure being the no-tobacco figure with the hazard ratio applied), oesophageal squamous cell cancer 16 with no tobacco and 55 with snus (HR 3.5, 1.6–7.6; one cohort, 10 exposed cases), pancreatic cancer at 27 years 72 and 151 (RR 2.1, 1.2–3.3; 18 exposed cases), and cancer deaths 2,141 and 2,395, which is 2.1 and 2.4 in 100 men (editors' conversion; the row comes from Byhamre et al.), with raised ratios also for non-cardia stomach cancer (HR 1.4, 1.1–1.9) and rectal cancer (1.38, 1.07–1.77). Its authors rated these moderate certainty for the oesophagus and for the pancreas at 27 years and low for the others; the pancreatic ratio was 1.07 (0.77–1.50) in a pooled analysis over 36 years (very low), the rectal ratio 1.10 (0.91–1.34) with longer follow-up, and oral cancer (0.93, 0.59–1.44), lung cancer (0.8, 0.4–1.3) and colon cancer (1.08, 0.91–1.29) showed no clear difference. A narrative review supported by Swedish Match, a snus maker, and written by a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry (Lee, 2013) concluded that adverse health effects of snus have not been clearly identified and that any cancer risk is at most minimal and much less than that of smoking; it pooled heart attack in never-smoking Swedish men to RR 1.07 (0.98–1.16), or 1.00 (0.91–1.10) without one 1971–74 estimate, while its own results also show fatal heart attack 1.31 (1.09–1.58) against non-fatal 0.89 (0.79–1.00), heart failure up to 2.08 (1.03–4.22), and poorer survival after a cancer diagnosis in men who used snus only (1.13, 1.05–1.20), though less so than in men who smoked only (1.21, 1.17–1.25). IARC (2012) judged smokeless tobacco as a class carcinogenic to humans (Group 1: oral cavity, oesophagus, pancreas) without separating products, and notes that Swedish snus is made with extra controls on nitrosamines and that four northern-European studies of oral cancer found no overall association. A 2026 systematic review without meta-analysis, rated critically low confidence by the editors (Kopa-Stojak, 2026), describes pooled heart attack, stroke, atrial fibrillation and pancreatic cancer estimates near 1 (1.04, 1.04, 1.07, 0.96) beside fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06–1.55) and heart failure 2.08 (1.03–4.22). Against smoking the sources give little: Byhamre et al. left out men who had ever regularly smoked; Valen et al. report cancer estimates higher for smoking than for snus at most sites in the same studies, with overlapping intervals except for lung (Figure 4, not read as numbers), and say it is not known how far switching from smoking to snus reduces the benefit of stopping all tobacco; no source read compares the overall death rate of men who use snus with that of people who smoke, and the figure of no more than 1% of the effects of smoking in Lee's Discussion comes from his 2011 review, which was not read. These sources overlap heavily (the Swedish construction-worker cohort sits inside most estimates), tobacco use was recorded once at the start, women are almost absent, few men were followed beyond 70, and none of these studies can show that snus caused the differences. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: In large studies of Swedish men who had never smoked, using snus was linked to a death rate 28% higher than in men who used no tobacco, once age and weight were allowed for (hazard ratio 1.28; 1.27 for deaths from heart and blood-vessel disease). Over the years studied, 2.1 in 100 men who used no tobacco died of cancer; with the snus ratio applied, that becomes about 2.4 in 100. Cancers of the gullet (oesophagus) and pancreas were rare but more frequent in men who used snus: for the gullet, about 55 in 100,000 against 16 in 100,000 men who used no tobacco. Mouth and lung cancer showed no clear difference, and some results shrank with longer follow-up. A review supported by a snus maker concluded that harm has not been clearly identified; independent studies found the raised figures above. These studies cannot show that snus caused the differences, nearly all the men were Swedish, men who used snus drank more alcohol, and no study read measured how snus compares with smoking in deaths overall; for cancers, the figures for smoking were higher at most sites.
population: Men in Sweden who had never smoked, in cohorts recruited from the 1970s to 2010 (one dominant construction-worker cohort), with Norwegian cohort data in IARC's review, and in reviews of such studies; no data on women beyond one lymphoma estimate
exposure: Using snus (moist smokeless tobacco as made in Sweden), recorded once at the start of each study; mostly snus with no other tobacco
comparator: Men who never used any tobacco (the main comparison in every study read); men who formerly used snus; men who smoked (indirect, from the few comparisons within the same studies)
outcome: Death from any cause, from cardiovascular disease and from cancer; cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas and rectum; heart attack and heart failure; survival after a cancer diagnosis; and what IARC concludes for smokeless tobacco as a class
magnitude: Byhamre et al. 2021 (eight Swedish cohorts; never-smoking men; 124,256 never used tobacco, 39,156 current snus only, 5,691 former snus only; adjusted for attained age and body mass index): current snus only against never used, all-cause HR 1.28 (1.20–1.35; 1,410 deaths against 9,272), cardiovascular 1.27 (1.15–1.41; 443 against 3,444), cancer 1.12 (1.00–1.26; 332 against 2,660), other causes 1.37 (1.24–1.52; 511 against 2,098) (the groups differ in age, so death counts are not comparable between them; no absolute rates are printed); former snus only: all-cause 1.15 (1.02–1.31), cancer 1.26 (1.01–1.57), cardiovascular 1.13 (0.91–1.41), other causes 1.14 (0.89–1.45). By years of use, all-cause under 5 years 1.08 (0.88–1.32), 5–9 1.17 (1.00–1.36), 10–14 1.31 (1.12–1.52), 15 or more 1.29 (1.20–1.38), p for trend 0.001; by weekly amount 1.28, 1.17, 1.37, p for trend 0.09. Sensitivity: without the Construction Worker Cohort 1.42 (1.21–1.66), cardiovascular 1.39 (1.05–1.84), cancer 1.52 (1.15–1.99); follow-up capped at 10 years 1.34 (1.21–1.48), cardiovascular 1.13 (0.93–1.38); extra adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity in six cohorts (158 snus-group deaths) 1.46 (1.22–1.75). Valen et al. 2023 (snus only against no tobacco; absolute risks per 100,000 men over each study's follow-up as in the review's table, no tobacco then snus, the snus figure being the no-tobacco figure with the hazard ratio applied): oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 16 then 55, HR 3.5 (1.6–7.6), moderate; pancreas at 27 years 72 then 151, RR 2.1 (1.2–3.3 in the table, 1.2–3.6 in the text), moderate, and HR 1.07 (0.77–1.50) at 36 years, very low; non-cardia stomach 237 then 332, HR 1.4 (1.1–1.9), low; rectum 339 then 468, HR 1.38 (1.07–1.77), low, and 1.10 (0.91–1.34) with longer follow-up; cancer deaths 2,141 then 2,395 (2.1 then 2.4 in 100 men, editors' conversion), HR 1.12 (1.00–1.26), low; oral cancer 0.93 (0.59–1.44), very low; lung RR 0.8 (0.4–1.3); colon HR 1.08 (0.91–1.29); all melanoma incidence rate ratio 0.65 (0.52–0.82). After a cancer diagnosis in construction workers: total mortality HR 1.13 (1.05–1.20), cancer death 1.15 (1.05–1.26). Lee 2013 (never-smoking Swedish men): heart attack or ischaemic heart disease, 13 estimates pooled, fixed-effect RR 1.07 (0.98–1.16), 1.00 (0.91–1.10) without the 1971–74 estimate; fatal heart attack 1.31 (1.09–1.58), non-fatal 0.89 (0.79–1.00); heart failure 1.28 (1.00–1.64; 75 exposed cases) and 2.08 (1.03–4.22; 14 cases); survival after a cancer diagnosis, all-cause RR 1.13 (1.05–1.20) snus only, 1.21 (1.17–1.25) smoking only, 1.17 (1.12–1.22) both; cancer-specific 1.15 (1.05–1.26) against 1.15 (1.10–1.21). IARC 2012: smokeless tobacco Group 1; northern-Europe oral cancer pooled 1.0 (0.7–1.3); Swedish oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma RR 3.5 (1.6–7.6); pancreas Norway 1.67 (1.12–2.50; 45 cases; 0.85, 0.24–3.07, in people who never smoked) and Swedish construction workers 2.1 (1.2–3.6; 18 cases), pooled 1.8 (1.3–2.5). Kopa-Stojak 2026 (as described, from primary analyses): heart attack 1.04 (0.93–1.17); fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06–1.55); stroke 1.04 (0.92–1.17), death after stroke 1.32 (1.08–1.61); atrial fibrillation 1.07 (0.97–1.19); heart failure 2.08 (1.03–4.22) and 1.28 (1.00–1.64); cardiovascular death 1.70 (1.01–2.87) in people who used snus and never used tobacco; pancreatic cancer 0.96 (0.83–1.11) pooled against 2.0 (1.2–3.3) in one cohort; rectal cancer 1.40 (1.09–1.79).

evidence.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Eight Swedish cohorts (recruited 1978 to 2010), men only, anyone who had ever regularly smoked cigarettes excluded: 169,103 men, 2,857,312 person-years (about 17 years each, editors' calculation), 10,928 deaths. 124,256 men (73.5%) had never used tobacco and 39,156 (23%) currently used snus and no other tobacco; 5,691 had formerly used snus and no other tobacco (in the cohorts that recorded former use). Tobacco use was recorded once, at baseline.

evidence.locator: Table 3, duration and amount rows; Results, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Among men who currently used snus and no other tobacco, against never-users of tobacco, by years of snus use at baseline, all-cause aHR rose from 1.08 (0.88–1.32) under 5 years to 1.29 (1.20–1.38) at 15 years or more (p for trend 0.001); cardiovascular and other-cause deaths showed the same pattern (p for trend 0.001 each), cancer did not (0.11). evidence.locator: Table 2; Discussion, 4th to 7th, 8th and 10th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The current snus group was younger (mean age 29 against 38 years), drank more (37.9% in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2%) and more often had 10 to 12 years of education (52.6% against 38.7%) than men who never used tobacco (the alcohol and education percentages are within the cohorts that recorded them, which leaves out the Construction Workers Cohort); body mass index was similar (24.1 against 24.6). The authors name residual confounding and a single baseline measurement of exposure as weaknesses, and describe their findings as supporting an association, with public-health relevance if it is causal. Their suggested explanations (nicotine effects on blood vessels and heart rhythm, tumour promotion, poorer cancer survival, alcohol-linked injury and violence, risk-taking) were not tested in these data.

evidence.extracted: The authors' summary: snus probably increases the risk of cancer of the oesophagus and pancreas (moderate certainty), may increase the risk of stomach and rectal cancer (low), and the evidence suggests more cancer deaths and more deaths after a cancer diagnosis (low); they are very uncertain about the other cancers, and do not know the effect in women. evidence.extracted: Studies by researchers linked to the tobacco industry or sponsored by it were excluded by design, as were estimates based only on combined snus and cigarette use. Exposure caveats: a single baseline recording of tobacco habits; about 30% of exclusive snus users may later stop or move to smoking (a Swedish study cited); in the paragraph on the Construction Workers Cohort, more than 75% of exclusive snus users were under 30 at entry, against 31% of smokers, and only a small proportion of snus users were traced beyond 70; seven of the included studies used construction-worker data from 1971 to 1975, when non-use could not be told from non-response; 13.2% of never-smoking snus users, against 6.7% of never users of tobacco, had a repeat record showing smoking in one study. All authors declare no conflicts of interest; the page has no funding statement.

risk_of_bias.note: Byhamre et al. (card sc_byhamre_2021: ROBINS-E overall high): the main model adjusts for age and body mass index only, tobacco use was recorded once, and the snus group was younger and drank more, so residual confounding could change the ratios materially. Valen et al. rated all 15 of their studies moderate risk of bias, mostly for the validity of exposure information; Lee (2013) and IARC (2012) are narrative reviews and Lee's is industry-supported (editors' checklist, cards sc_lee_2013 and sc_iarc_2012). Counted once for the confounding problem.

inconsistency.note: The sources read the same cohorts differently: Lee concludes adverse effects have not been clearly identified, while the independent review and IARC find raised cancer estimates. Within the data, estimates fall with longer follow-up (pancreas 2.1 at 27 years, 1.07 at 36 years; rectum 1.38, 1.10; cardiovascular 1.27, 1.13 at a 10-year cap), and heart attack incidence (1.04–1.07) differs from fatal heart attack (1.28–1.31). Part is explained by the dominant cohort and part is not.

indirectness.note: Men only, almost all Swedish, in one dominant occupational cohort recruited from the 1970s with tobacco use measured once; snus made before 1983 differs from later products and from snus elsewhere (IARC); the comparison with smoking is indirect (no cohort read compares death rates of men who use only snus with men who smoke; Byhamre et al. left out men who had smoked regularly).

imprecision.note: All-cause and cancer-death ratios are precise (10,928 deaths), but the site-specific cancer estimates rest on 10 to 73 exposed cases with wide intervals (oesophagus 3.5, 1.6–7.6; oral 0.93, 0.59–1.44) and the absolute risks are the review's, per 100,000 men, with the snus figure derived from the no-tobacco figure.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources. The independent review excluded industry-linked studies by design, which is stated; the industry-supported review is read beside it.

large_effect.note: The oesophageal ratio (3.5) rests on 10 exposed cases in one cohort and the all-cause ratio (1.28) is not large; no upgrade.

dose_response.note: The all-cause ratio rises with years of use (p for trend 0.001) but not clearly with weekly amount (p for trend 0.09; cardiovascular highest in the lightest group); years of use also follows age and cohort; no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Men who used snus drank more alcohol, so residual confounding would more plausibly raise than lower the ratios; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is downgraded one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: an association in never-smoking men, snus only against no tobacco; whether it is causal is a separate and unresolved question. The ratings in the Valen et al. review (moderate for the oesophagus and for the pancreas at 27 years, low for stomach, rectum and cancer deaths, very low for most others) are its authors' judgments from a different starting point and are reported, not adopted. Overlapping reports are counted once: the Swedish construction-worker cohort sits inside Byhamre et al., Valen et al., Lee, IARC and Kopa-Stojak, Valen et al.'s mortality row is the Byhamre analysis, and the survival-after-cancer result in Lee and in Valen et al. is the same study, so the agreement between them is not independent replication and the status is contested, not replicated.

debate.question: Does using snus make men who never smoked more likely to die, or to get certain cancers, than men who use no tobacco, and how large is any difference compared with smoking?
debate.evidence_yes: The largest pooled cohort analysis (Byhamre et al., 2021; 169,103 never-smoking Swedish men, 10,928 deaths; funded by a university department, Swedish regional authorities and a medical society; no conflicts declared) found that men who used snus only died at a rate 28% higher than men who never used tobacco (HR 1.28, 1.20–1.35), with the ratio rising with years of use (1.08, 0.88–1.32, under 5 years; 1.29, 1.20–1.38, at 15 years or more; p for trend 0.001) and staying raised in the sensitivity analyses (1.42 without the largest cohort; 1.46 with extra adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity in six cohorts; 1.34 with follow-up capped at 10 years); former snus use was also linked to a higher rate (1.15, 1.02–1.31). An independent systematic review that left out tobacco-industry-linked studies (Valen et al., 2023; no conflicts declared, no funding statement on the page) rated the evidence moderate certainty that snus raises the risk of oesophageal and pancreatic cancer (HR 3.5, 1.6–7.6; RR 2.1, 1.2–3.3) and low for stomach and rectal cancer and for cancer deaths, and reported poorer survival after a cancer diagnosis (1.13, 1.05–1.20). IARC (2012) found sufficient evidence that smokeless tobacco as a class causes cancers of the oral cavity, oesophagus and pancreas, and weighed the same Swedish oesophageal (3.5) and pancreatic (2.1) findings with a Norwegian pancreatic cohort at 1.67 (1.12–2.50). Even the industry-supported review's own results show fatal heart attack 1.31 (1.09–1.58) with non-fatal 0.89, heart failure up to 2.08 (1.03–4.22) and poorer survival after a cancer diagnosis; the 2026 systematic review lists fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06–1.55) and cardiovascular death 1.70 (1.01–2.87) in people who used snus and never used any tobacco.
debate.evidence_no: The industry-supported narrative review (Lee, 2013; supported by Swedish Match, a snus maker, with earlier reviews supported by Philip Morris Products and the European Smokeless Tobacco Council; the author is a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry and the paper says the sponsor was not involved) concludes that adverse health effects have not been clearly identified and that any cancer risk is at most minimal and far below that of smoking; it pools heart attack in never-smoking men to 1.07 (0.98–1.16), or 1.00 (0.91–1.10) leaving out one 1971–74 estimate, and lists cancers of the oropharynx, oesophagus, stomach and lung as unassociated. Parts of the independent evidence also point to a small or null effect: four northern-European oral-cancer studies found no overall association (IARC; pooled 1.0, 0.7–1.3); only one of four northern-European oesophageal studies was significant; Valen et al. found no clear difference for oral (0.93, 0.59–1.44), lung (0.8, 0.4–1.3) or colon cancer, a pooled pancreatic ratio of 1.07 (0.77–1.50) at 36 years and a rectal ratio of 1.10 (0.91–1.34) with longer follow-up; Byhamre et al. found the cardiovascular ratio no longer different from 1 with follow-up capped at 10 years (1.13, 0.93–1.38), and describe an association whose public-health relevance holds only if it is causal. The 2026 systematic review lists pooled heart attack (1.04), stroke (1.04), atrial fibrillation (1.07) and pancreatic cancer (0.96, 0.83–1.11) near no difference, though the editors rate its confidence critically low and its abstract reads several of these null results as increases.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether snus causes any of the differences: tobacco use was recorded once at the start, men who used snus drank more (37.9% in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2%) and were younger, the main model adjusted for age and body mass index only, 13.2% of never-smoking men who used snus against 6.7% of men who never used tobacco had a later record showing smoking in one study, and about 30% of men using snus only may later stop or move to smoking (a Swedish study cited by Valen et al.). Whether the findings hold for women (one lymphoma estimate, no cases), young people, men over 70, other countries or today's products; Swedish snus made before 1983 was fermented and differs from later products (IARC). How the overall death rate of men who use snus compares with that of people who smoke: no source read measures it, and the figure of no more than 1% of the effects of smoking comes from a 2011 review that was not read. How far the sources are independent: the Swedish construction-worker cohort supplies most of the deaths in Byhamre et al. (87% in the snus group), most participants in Valen et al.'s pooled analyses (two thirds, and 72% of pancreatic cases) and several of the estimates in the other three, and Valen et al.'s mortality row is the Byhamre analysis, so agreement between them is not independent replication. The industry-supported review and the independent ones draw largely on the same cohorts, so many of their differences come from how the same data are read, not from different data.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From the sources read: in Swedish men who never smoked, the largest pooled analysis finds a death rate 28% higher in men who used snus only than in men who never used tobacco, and an independent systematic review finds more oesophageal and pancreatic cancer in single cohorts (moderate certainty by its authors) and probably more stomach and rectal cancer and cancer deaths (low); other estimates, such as oral and lung cancer, show no clear difference. The sources agree on more than their headlines suggest: Lee and Valen et al. both judge the cancer risk of snus to be below that of smoking, both report the same poorer survival after a cancer diagnosis in construction workers who used snus (1.13), and the industry-supported review's own results include a raised fatal heart attack figure. They differ on the cancers: Lee concludes that adverse effects have not been clearly identified, while IARC (a verdict on smokeless tobacco as a class) and Valen et al. judge a cancer hazard probable, and the pancreatic estimate fell from 2.1 at 27 years to 1.07 in a 36-year pooled analysis whose follow-up runs to 2013, after the search dates of both Lee and IARC. The strongest argument for a raised risk is the consistency of the all-cause ratio across sensitivity analyses (1.28 to 1.46) and its rise with years of use; the strongest against is that the cancer-site results rest on few cases from one cohort and shrink with longer follow-up, that confounding is possible, and that the sources overlap. The editors give no number for how snus compares with smoking in deaths overall, because none of the sources read measures it. Both halves belong together: for cancers, the estimates in these studies are lower for snus than for smoking, and they are not zero.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Cohorts that measure tobacco use repeatedly over decades, adjust fully (alcohol, education, diet, early-life factors), include women and younger and older men, and report absolute rates for men who use snus only, men who smoke, men who used both and men who used neither, so that the comparison with smoking can be read directly; analyses outside the construction-worker cohort with enough cases for the oesophagus and pancreas (10 and 18 exposed cases in the main estimates), and follow-up beyond 36 years; designs that handle confounding, such as comparisons of siblings or of men who stopped; and a pre-specified systematic review that includes industry-supported and independent studies and appraises both with the same tool. None of the sources read reports these.
